w: August 1833: Parliament voted freedom for the empire’s enslaved people, paying a vast fortune in compensation to former owners rather than to the freed.

March 1867: Secretary Seward paid 7.2 million dollars for a territory mocked as a frozen wasteland, a bargain at roughly two cents an acre. The Klondike gold rush three decades later made the mockery look foolish.
July 20, 1969 — Armstrong’s boot, a camera left behind to watch, and 600 million viewers.
April 1, 1976 — three founders; the first product was a bare circuit board.

November 11, 1918: the guns stopped on the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month, and the celebrating hid how little the peace would hold. The war had unmade four empires and killed perhaps sixteen million people.
October 29, 1969 — "LO." The intended "LOGIN" crashed the system after two letters.
August 16, 1858: the new cable under the Atlantic carried 99 words of congratulation in an hour, plus celebration fireworks and parades, and then died within weeks. The 1866 cable stuck, and stayed.
January 1926: in a London attic, Baird showed a flickering human face to a Royal Institution audience. A decade later the world was watching broadcasts, and the flicker never stopped.
October 25, 1415, St. Crispin’s Day: mud, arrows, and a French charge that bogged down ankle-deep. Shakespeare gave the king a better speech than the field did, but not by much.

June 1314: a smaller Scottish army trapped the English cavalry in boggy ground between the Bannock and the Forth. The victory secured Scottish independence for a generation, though the formal treaty waited until 1328.
October 14, 1066. Harold died late in the day, and by Christmas a French-speaking duke was being crowned in Westminster.
November 9, 1989 — a botched press conference and guards who stopped taking orders.
Autumn 1347, at Messina — within five years perhaps a third of the continent was gone.

January 1959: Batista fled at dawn on New Year’s Day, and Castro’s column took a week to walk the island’s length, cheered the whole way. The revolution’s turn toward the Soviet bloc came within two years.
December 25, 800. Pope Leo III set the crown on his head during the Mass, and Byzantium spent centuries refusing to applaud.
April 26, 1986 — the announcement began with Swedish monitors noticing radiation that wasn’t theirs.
September 6, 1522: the Victoria limped into Seville with fewer than 20 of the original crew, and without Magellan, who had died in the Philippines.
October 12, 1492 — an island in the Bahamas he insisted on calling the Indies.
From late 1814 the powers danced through a year of balls and bargaining; the settlement they wrote kept Europe’s borders mostly quiet for a hundred years.
August 6, 2012 — the seven minutes of terror, a sky-crane hover, and it stuck the landing.
June 6, 1944 — the largest seaborne invasion in history, on five beaches and from the air.
Nuremberg, 1543: printed as he lay dying, it argued that Earth turns around the Sun. Nearly a century passed before Kepler and Galileo settled the argument in the book’s favor.
Philadelphia, July 4, 1776 — news crossed the Atlantic by sailing ship, weeks later.

December 1898: the Curies named the new element for the rays it gave off on its own. Marie Curie processed tonnes of pitchblende by hand to isolate a speck of it, and the work slowly cost her her life.
March 1889 — critics called it a "useless and monstrous" tower. It was meant to come down in 1909.

January 1649: a king was beheaded outside his own banqueting house, by a court whose authority he refused to recognize. The monarchy and the House of Lords were abolished within weeks, and Britain became a republic for eleven years.
May 29, 1453: gunpowder finally beat the Theodosian Walls, Constantine XI died in the breach, and the city became Istanbul, capital of an empire that would rule from the Danube to the Nile.
April 30, 1975 — helicopters lifting off rooftops, the war’s most famous photograph taken from below.
March 6, 1836: the garrison was overrun before dawn, and Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie died with it. Remember the Alamo became the rally of the Texas Revolution, settled weeks later at San Jacinto.
September 4, 476: the teenage Romulus Augustulus was packed off to a pension in Campania, the regalia went east to Zeno, and a barbarian officer ruled Italy.
July 1099: after a five-week siege the crusaders took the city, and an armed pilgrimage had become a conquest. The Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem lasted less than a century before Saladin took it back.
May 29, 1953: the ninth British expedition to the mountain was the one that stood on it. They spent about fifteen minutes on top, and left a hole in the snow for someone else to find.
April 1896 — 14 nations, no women athletes, and a marathon winner who became a Greek national hero.

May 1796: Jenner inoculated eight-year-old James Phipps with matter from a milkmaid’s cowpox sore, later with smallpox itself, and the boy stayed well. The word vaccine descends from vacca, the Latin for cow.
July–August 1914 — a Sarajevo assassination lit a fuse the whole alliance system had laid.
April 1861 — the bombardment lasted a day and a half; the war lasted four years.
May 6, 1954: on a windy Oxford track, Bannister ran a mile in 3:59.4 with two pacemakers. Doctors had called the barrier impossible; within weeks it was merely difficult.
July 14, 1789 — seven prisoners freed, one revolution begun.
April 12, 1961: one lap of the Earth in 108 minutes, and a 27-year-old test pilot became the most famous man alive. The flight lasted a single morning, and it gave the Space Age its first hero.
January 1610: four little stars that shuffled around Jupiter broke the Earth-centered sky for good. Naming them the Medicean stars was politics; the orbits were physics.
January 30, 1948: shot on his way to a prayer meeting by a Hindu nationalist, a martyr at 78. His ashes went to the rivers of India; his fasting had already stopped a civil war.
January 18, 1871: proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors while Paris lay under siege, chosen as the spot so France would never forget.

May 1, 1851: the world’s first world’s fair, a glass house built of mass-produced parts in months, drew six million visitors in half a year. The profits founded Kensington’s museum quarter, which was the point.

Autumn 1845: a fungus reached Ireland and the food of millions rotted in the fields. In seven years about a million people died and two million emigrated, and the island never regained its population.
September 2 to 6, 1666, starting in a bakery in Pudding Lane. It consumed 13,000 houses and 87 churches, and it broke the plague year’s back.
November 5, 1605 — thirty-six barrels of gunpowder under Parliament.
Mainz, around 1455 — about 180 copies, and Europe was never private again.
A lawsuit from 1439 had already let slip the secret press; by 1440 he was back at Mainz, and fifteen years later the Bible changed everything.
August 1791: the richest colony in the Americas rose against slavery itself. Thirteen years of war ended with Haiti, the first Black republic, independent in 1804.
May 6, 1937 — "Oh, the humanity!" — 97 people aboard; 62 survived.
April 1990 — its first images were blurry; a 1993 servicing mission gave it glasses.

August 1981: IBM built its PC from off-the-shelf parts and licensed the operating system from a young company called Microsoft. The clones that followed made the architecture universal, and the licensing made Microsoft rich.
June 1325, aged 21. By traditional count he covered some 75,000 miles across the Muslim world and beyond, several times Marco Polo’s route.

June 1812: more than half a million men crossed the Niemen, the largest army Europe had ever assembled. Fewer than one in ten came back; the retreat destroyed the myth of invincibility that had held the empire together.
June 29, 2007 — lines around Apple Stores; the App Store didn’t even exist until a year later.

May 1607: about a hundred colonists anchored on a marshy island in the James River and named the place for their king. The starving years that followed killed most of them, and the colony survived by learning to grow tobacco.
November 22, 1963 — the Zapruder film exists because a dressmaker brought his camera to Dealey Plaza.
October 7, 1571, in the Gulf of Patras: the Holy League’s galleys broke the Ottoman line in a single afternoon; a young Cervantes sailed in it and lost the use of his left hand.
April 1865: Lee surrendered at Appomattox on the 9th, and Lincoln was shot on the 14th. The war ended and the fight over its meaning began.
May 1927 — 33 and a half hours, dead reckoning, and a periscope because he couldn’t see past the fuel tank.
1803 — 828,000 square miles from Napoleon for about four cents an acre.
August 10, 1793, with 537 paintings on the walls, most of them confiscated from the crown. A palace became public property in an afternoon.

September 1519: five ships and about 270 men left Spain. One ship and 18 men returned three years later, without Magellan, who died in the Philippines, and the voyage proved the globe could be sailed around.
Runnymede, June 1215 — the king first put his seal under the law. He ignored it within weeks.
May 1994 — a fully representative election, four years after leaving prison.

December 1620: after a brutal crossing and a winter that killed half of them, the survivors built a village on a bay where a Wampanoag settlement had stood, emptied by plague years before. Their compact for self-government was signed before anyone stepped ashore.

April 1742: Handel staged his new oratorio for two Dublin charities, and the audience was asked to leave swords and hooped skirts at home so more people would fit. London took years to accept sacred words in a theatre, but the Hallelujah Chorus never left.

1905: a patent clerk in Bern published four papers that remade physics, covering light, atoms, time, and mass. Any one of them would have made a career; together they redirected the century’s science.
October 1908 — "any color so long as it is black" came later; the price kept falling instead.
Florence, about 1503 — he carried it with him for the rest of his life.
August 1920 — 72 years after Seneca Falls, decided by one state legislator’s mother’s advice.
Wittenberg, October 1517 — the split that remade Europe began as a complaint about indulgences.
November 1859 — the first printing of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers on day one.
June 1381: Wat Tyler’s army camped on Blackheath, burned the duke of Lancaster’s palace, and met the boy king face to face at Mile End.
September 1928 — a stack of forgotten petri dishes, one careless summer, one lucky mold.

September 13, 1759: a short fight outside the city walls killed both generals within days of each other. France kept a shell of its empire in North America until 1763, when it handed nearly all of it to Britain.
1687, paid for out of Edmond Halley’s own pocket — the laws of motion and universal gravitation.
Spring 1848: barricades rose in a dozen capitals and kings ran for the coast. By autumn nearly everywhere had been rolled back, but nothing was quite the same.
December 1, 1955: her arrest began a 381-day boycott that carried a 26-year-old pastor named Martin Luther King Jr. onto the national stage.

July 1799: an officer of Napoleon’s expedition noticed a slab of black granite carrying hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek. Twenty-three years later Champollion read the top line, and Egypt’s sealed past opened.
July 1947 — a press release about a "flying disc," then a weather balloon, then fifty years of argument.
April 1204: a crusade that never reached the Holy Land gutted Christendom’s greatest city instead, and the Venetians sailed home with its bronze horses.
September 1, 1939 — the Luftwaffe hit Wieluń at 4:40 in the morning.
September 11, 2001 — the morning the towers fell and the century found its shape.
April 1564 — his actual birthday is unknown; the record is his baptism.
Brussels, October 1911: Einstein, Planck, Curie and Rutherford sat in one room to argue about quanta; the group photograph became the discipline’s academy portrait.
Summer 1588: 130 ships, unfavorable winds, fireships in the Calais roads, and North Sea storms that finished the job on the way home.
October 4, 1957 — a polished 58cm sphere that beeped at the whole world at once.
May 1703 — a new capital raised from a swamp, by imperial decree.
September 1825 — Locomotion No. 1 pulled the first fare-paying passengers.
November 1869 — it cut the London-to-Bombay run by thousands of miles.
March 1876 — the same day he made the famous call to his assistant: "Mr. Watson, come here."
April 15, 1912 — over 1,500 died in water just below freezing. The Californian never answered.
October 21, 1805, off Cape Trafalgar: Nelson’s two columns cut the combined fleet apart, and he died below decks as the victory was sealed.

September 3, 1783: signed in Paris almost two years after the guns stopped at Yorktown, it gave the United States everything to the Mississippi River and fishing rights off Newfoundland, which the new country would soon need more than it knew.
July 16, 1945 — "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds." Oppenheimer said he thought of it later.
November 1922 — "wonderful things" glimpsed through a small breach by candlelight.
October 1929 — Black Thursday, then Black Monday, then Black Tuesday, then a decade of it.
June 18, 1815 — four days later he abdicated; the exile to Saint Helena followed.
December 17, 1903 — four flights at Kitty Hawk; the longest lasted 59 seconds.
